en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now at that time, the Venerable Nanda—the Blessed One’s maternal cousin—was handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring; he had been made by the Blessed One to have hair on his limbs only four finger-breadths long.
He wore a robe of the same measurement as the Sugata’s robe.
The elder monks saw the Venerable Nanda coming from afar.
Seeing him,
they rose from their seats, thinking, "The Blessed One is coming.
When they realized he had arrived, they grumbled, complained, and expressed their indignation:
“How can the Venerable Nanda wear a robe the size of the Sugata’s robe?
… [and so on] … “Is it true, Nanda, that you wear a robe the size of the Sugata’s robe?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, Nanda, wear a robe of the same measure as the Sugata’s robe?
This, Nanda, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of the faith of those who have it…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Whatever monk should have a robe made to the measure of the Sugata’s robe, or exceeding it, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down.
Herein, this is the measure of the Sugata’s robe: nine spans in length according to the Sugata’s span, and six spans across."
“This is the measure of the Sugata’s Sugata-cīvara.
“But whoever,” means whoever of such a kind... [and so on].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"The measure of a Sugata’s robe" means:
In length it is nine spans of the Sugata-span; in width, six spans.
"Should have made" means: either makes it herself or has it made; for the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having cut it off by means of obtaining [the material], a *pācittiya* offense is to be confessed.
If one brings to completion what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one brings to completion what was begun by oneself through others, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one brings to completion by oneself what has been partially constructed by others, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one brings to completion by others what has been partially constructed by others, there is an offense of expiation.
If one makes it or causes it to be made for the sake of another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one obtains and uses what has been made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense if one makes it deficient.
If, having obtained something made by another, he cuts it up and uses it—
whether as a canopy, a floor-covering, a wattle fence, a mattress, or a pillow—
for one who is insane;
"For the first offender.
The tenth training rule concerning Nanda is finished.
The ninth chapter, the Chapter on Jewels, is concluded.
Its summary verse:
The king and his treasure,
the needle, the bed, and the mattress.
"The sitting mat, the itch,
and the *vassikā* [flower] by the Sugata.
Venerable sirs, the ninety-two *pācittiya* rules have been recited.
In this matter, I ask the venerable ones:
"Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: [Are you pure in this?]
“Are you pure in this matter?
A third time I ask:
“Are you pure in this matter?”
"Venerable sirs, this matter is pure; therefore, you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The Minor Section is completed.
The Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation is finished.
